sections.heading: Looking for happiness in the right place
sections.text: Lord, teach me not to expect the world to give me the happiness only you can give. Keep me from believing that I will be freer or fuller if I live for myself. I know that my heart was made for you, and I will only be truly glad when my life is turned toward you.
theological_themes: True happiness is found in God, not in the world or self-centered living.
Human desires are rightly ordered only when God is their highest good.

scripture_references.connection: This psalm locates fullness of joy in God's presence, not in created things. It supports the prayer's claim that lasting happiness comes from God himself.
John contrasts love for the world with doing the will of God. The passage grounds the prayer's rejection of worldly happiness as temporary and spiritually dangerous.

sections.heading: Receiving the life you assign to me
sections.text: Help me want the life you give me, not the life I would design around my own comfort. Make me willing to do what you put in front of me, and to endure what you wisely allow. Teach me that if my life is not pleasing to you, it will never truly satisfy me either.
theological_themes: God's will is better than self-rule.
Obedience and even suffering under God's providence are part of a faithful life.
A life that displeases God cannot give deep satisfaction to the soul.

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers to offer their whole lives to God and to be transformed so they can discern and live out his will. This fits the prayer's movement from self-centered living to surrendered obedience.

Peter speaks of suffering according to God's will while continuing to do good and entrusting oneself to the Creator. This supports the prayer's desire to accept both doing and suffering what God assigns.

sections.heading: Wanting a heavenly mind in an earthly life
sections.text: Give me a heart like your servants in heaven, who gladly go wherever you send them and do what you command. Even while I live in this ordinary, lower world, keep my desires lifted toward you. Do not let earthly things take over my heart. Make me ready to serve here while belonging to you there.
theological_themes: Believers are called to obey God's will on earth with a heaven-shaped heart.
Earthly responsibilities are to be carried out without making earthly things ultimate.
The prayer uses angelic obedience as a model of prompt and willing service to God.

scripture_references.connection: The psalm describes angels and heavenly hosts as servants who do God's will. This directly supports the prayer's request for the same willing obedience.
Paul calls believers to set their minds on things above because their life is hidden with Christ. This grounds the prayer's desire to live faithfully on earth without being ruled by earthly desires.

sections.heading: Depending on you instead of myself
sections.text: Father, do not let me try to live this life in my own strength. I cannot make myself holy, fruitful, or faithful by willpower alone. Keep turning my eyes back to you. Give me the help I need, because apart from you I have nothing to offer and no power to become what you call me to be.
theological_themes: The Christian life cannot be lived by self-reliance.
Fruitfulness and holiness come through dependence on God.
Humility begins with admitting inability apart from grace.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that branches bear fruit only by abiding in him and that apart from him his disciples can do nothing. This is the clearest biblical grounding for the prayer's confession of dependence.
Paul holds together the believer's active obedience and God's prior, enabling work within them. This supports asking God for the power to live the life he commands.

sections.heading: Giving myself fully to you
sections.text: This is not a life I could ever choose or live unless you changed me. But it is the life every heart made alive by you longs to pursue. So make this my real concern: that I would belong to you without holding pieces of myself back. Take my time, my desires, my work, my suffering, my plans, and my future, and make them yours.
theological_themes: A God-centered life is the fruit of conversion and new spiritual life.
The believer presses on toward fuller devotion, even while not yet perfected.
Whole-life consecration belongs to genuine discipleship.

scripture_references.connection: Paul explains that the mind set on the flesh cannot submit to or please God, while believers belong to the Spirit. This supports the original distinction between the unconverted person and the godly soul pursuing this life.
Paul describes the Christian life as pressing on toward what lies ahead, not claiming perfection. This matches the prayer's desire to keep pursuing full devotion to God.

sections.heading: Asking for fruitfulness before time is gone
sections.text: Make me more alive to you, more fruitful, more spiritually awake. My lack of fruit weighs on me, and I do not want to waste the short time you have given me. It hurts to watch days pass with so little done that truly matters. So help me depend on you for every step of my growth, and for everything you intend to do in me, through me, in the world, and for your kingdom.
theological_themes: Spiritual barrenness is a real grief for a believer.
Time is precious and should be used in light of God's purposes.
Sanctification and usefulness in God's kingdom depend on God's grace and power.

scripture_references.connection: Paul prays that believers would walk in a way pleasing to the Lord, bearing fruit and being strengthened by God. This supports the request for greater fruitfulness and spiritual life.
Paul urges believers to walk wisely, making the best use of the time and understanding the Lord's will. This grounds the prayer's concern over wasted time and desire to live purposefully.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original says a person should desire to live in the world only to do and suffer what God allots. This assumes a strong doctrine of providence, including God's wise rule over hardship; some readers may find this pastorally difficult if applied carelessly to suffering.

The phrase 'no unconverted man can live' reflects the original's Puritan anthropology: apart from regeneration, a person cannot live a life truly pleasing to God. This is biblically defensible in texts such as Romans 8:7-9, but it is a doctrinally weighty claim and should not be softened into mere moral difficulty.

The original's reference to angels coming down to the 'lower world' carries an older cosmological and devotional framing. It has been retained as a biblical image of heavenly obedience rather than as speculation about angelic experience.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered 'happiness' as deep gladness and satisfaction in God, not as passing emotional cheerfulness, because the prayer contrasts God-centered life with worldly and self-centered sources of fulfillment.
I interpreted 'living to thee' as whole-life devotion expressed in ordinary obedience, suffering, work, desires, and use of time, rather than as withdrawal from earthly responsibilities.
I kept the original's concrete grief over 'barrenness' by naming lack of spiritual fruit as a burden, while avoiding language that could be confused with physical infertility.

I treated 'every accomplishment of thy purposes for me, for the world, and for thy kingdom' as dependence on God for sanctification and usefulness in his larger redemptive purposes, without implying that the individual can know every detail of God's plan.
